source.title: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper takes an empirical scaling-law loss parameterization as given and derives a compute allocation from it; it does not test the empirical scaling laws on language models.
record.gate_note: The paper describes empirical power laws and reports parameter estimates from cited work, but those are not its own results. Its own relevant result is the conditional analytical optimization in Proposition 4. Other scaling-law results cited in the text are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A theoretical synthesis. It assumes the Hoffmann et al. loss form (26) and R=6MD, then derives the compute-optimal allocation analytically (Proposition 4). It reports no language-model runs, no fits and no measured losses, so none of its own results bear empirically on any version. Its mechanism derivations (Propositions 1-2) are toy-model results, not tests of scaling in language models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' main conclusion is that the frequency and spectral mechanisms for power-law curves, developed in activity theory, were independently rediscovered in deep-learning scaling theory with matching exponent formulas. They also conclude that a curve's shape reflects mainly the environment's situation distribution, and that three mechanisms give indistinguishable curves, so curve shape cannot reveal the learner's structure. The compute allocation is a minor derived result, conditional on the assumed loss form.
record.recipe_differences: The paper offers a theoretical synthesis and conditional optimization, rather than reproducing the original empirical fitting procedure or running language-model scaling experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: In a toy experience-formation model, Zipf-distributed situations give a power-law learning curve with exponent β/(1+β); a uniform distribution gives an exponential. A gamma or power-law Hessian spectrum also gives power laws, so the mechanism cannot be identified from curve shape.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law scaling curves can arise from several distinct mechanisms that are indistinguishable from curve shape (theoretical, not an empirical LM test).

record.problems: No new language-model scaling measurements, run-level data, or empirical checks of the derived compute-optimal allocation are reported; the allocation depends on the assumed loss parameterization and compute relation.
record.rows_left_out: Cited empirical scaling-law findings and parameter estimates from references [30], [31], and [34] were left out because they are not results produced by this study.

untested.parts: No held-out LM loss measured or fitted.
Allocation is derived analytically from an assumed loss form; no empirical check.
No other modalities or regimes tested.
No fitting choices varied. Broken power laws are only cited [19].

record.verdict_notes: Peer-reviewed theory paper (Large-scale Systems Control, 2026). Its empirical scaling claims are all cited from Hestness, Kaplan and Hoffmann. No verdicts are given because the paper contains no empirical tests.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model losses are measured or fitted by the paper.
No extrapolation from smaller runs to larger runs is performed.
The paper derives an optimum conditional on an assumed loss form and compute relation, but does not empirically test the allocation trend or compare it across setups.
No other modalities or training regimes are experimentally tested.
No downstream task performance is evaluated.
The paper does not itself vary fitting choices or test whether fitted exponents or allocation trends change; mentioned results on broken power laws are cited from other work.

rows.subject: Scaling-law loss parameterization (26)
rows.operation_detail: Analytically minimizes the assumed loss function subject to the compute constraint R = 6MD.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal parameter-count and data-volume exponents as functions of the assumed loss exponents α and β.
rows.value: M* ∝ R^(β/(α+β)); D* ∝ R^(α/(α+β)). The text further gives cited empirical estimates α ≈ β ≈ 0.34, yielding M* ∝ R^(1/2) and D* ∝ R^(1/2).
rows.note: This is a conditional derivation, not a measurement of language-model runs. The α and β estimates are attributed to reference [31], not obtained in this paper.
rows.check: This is an analytical derivation conditional on an assumed loss form, not a measurement, so it should not be linked to V3 as evidence. The α≈β≈0.34 values are cited from Hoffmann et al. [31], an original source. The record's value also misreads the garbled text: it states M* ∝ R^(1/2), whereas the extracted text shows 'M* ∝ R' with a stray '1/2'. The derivation itself gives M* ∝ R^(β/(α+β)), which equals R^(1/2) when α=β.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
